**Surah al-Fatihah**

Qatadah said: it is Meccan. Mujahid said: it is Medinan.

It has three names: Fatihat al-Kitab (the Opening of the Book), Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an), and al-Sab' al-Mathani (the Seven Oft-Repeated).

Ibn Abi Dhi'b narrated from Sa'id al-Maqburi, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: "It is Umm al-Qur'an, it is Fatihat al-Kitab, and it is al-Sab' al-Mathani." As for its being called Fatihat al-Kitab, it is because the Book is opened with it in writing and with its recitation in speech.

As for its being called Umm al-Qur'an, it is because it comes first, and the rest of the surahs follow it. It became a "mother" (umm) because it precedes (amma) them, that is, it goes before them. In the same way, the battle standard is called umm because it leads and the army follows it. The poet said:

*Upon his head is a standard (umm), by which one is guided,*
*a gathering of affairs whose command is not disobeyed.*

It was also said that the years of a person's life that have passed are called an umm, because they came before.

The poet said:

*When fifty years have become your umm,*
*your opinion will be no better than that of a dying physician.*

There is a difference of opinion regarding calling it Umm al-Kitab. Most scholars permitted it, because al-Kitab is the Qur'an. al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin prohibited it, and they claimed that Umm al-Kitab is the name of the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), so no other thing should be called by it, based on the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book with Us, exalted and full of wisdom﴾ [az-Zukhruf 43:4].

As for calling Makkah Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Towns), there are two views:

The first: it was called so because it precedes all other towns.

The second: it was called so because the earth was spread out (dahiya) from it and originated from it, so it became a "mother" to it, due to the earth's origin from it, as a child originates from its mother.

As for calling it al-Sab' al-Mathani, it is because it has seven verses according to all scholars.

As for the second meaning, it is because it is repeated (tuthanna) in every prayer, whether obligatory or voluntary. There is nothing in calling it al-Mathani that prevents calling anything else by this name. A'sha Hamdan said:

*So enter the mosque and call upon your Lord,*
*and study these al-Mathani and al-Tuwal.*

(p. 47)

***

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾. The scholars agreed that it is part of the Qur'an in Surah an-Naml. They differed only regarding its inclusion at the beginning of al-Fatihah and at the beginning of every surah. al-Shafi'i affirmed it in one group, and Abu Hanifah negated it in another.

There is a difference regarding the word bism (name). Abu 'Ubaydah and a group said that it is an extra particle (silah za'idah), and that the phrase is only "Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." They cited the verse of Labid:

*Until the year is complete; then peace be upon you both,*
*and whoever weeps for a full year has made an excuse.*

Here the mention of "peace" (al-salam) is extra, and the intended meaning is: "then peace be upon you both."

Those who held this view differed regarding the purpose of this addition, in two views:

The first: to honour and magnify His mention, so that a distinction is made by it between His mention and the mention of other created beings. This is the view of Qutrub.

The second: so that it leaves the ruling of an oath (qasam) for the purpose of seeking blessing (tabarruk). This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The majority held that bism is an essential, intended element. They differed regarding the meaning of the preposition bi (in/with) attached to it, whether it is in the sense of a command or of a statement, in two views:

(p. 48)

The first: it is in the sense of a command, and its implied meaning is: "Begin in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is in the sense of a report, and its implied meaning is: "I begin in the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful." This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The alif of connection (alif al-wasl) is omitted, joined in pronunciation and in writing, due to its frequent use, just as it is omitted from al-Rahman. It was not omitted in writing in the saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ [al-'Alaq 96:1], because this usage is rare.

The ism (noun/name) is a word that indicates the thing named by way of indication (dalalat isharah). The sifah (attribute/descriptive word) is a word that indicates the qualified thing by way of informing (dalalat ifadah). If you make the sifah an ism, it indicates both matters: indication and information.

A group claimed that the ism is the essence of the named thing, and that the word is the act of naming, not the ism. This is corrupt, because if the names of essences were the essences themselves, then the names of actions would be the actions themselves. This is impossible regarding actions, so it is impossible regarding essences.

They differed regarding the derivation of ism, in two views: The first: it is derived from simah, which means a mark, because the ism distinguishes the named thing. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: it is derived from sumuw, which means elevation, because the ism rises (yasmu) by means of the named thing, and so elevates it above others. This is the view of al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj.

He quoted the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

*If you cannot achieve a matter, leave it,*
*and pass on to what you can do,*
*and connect it with supplication, for every matter*
*that rises above you, or that you rise toward, is a longing.*

Whoever considered the meanings of the letters in bism Allah formed an interpretation, applying to it the meaningful rulings of the letters, so that it became intended whenever Allah is mentioned in every naming. They have three sayings regarding this:

The first: the ba' (b) is His splendour (bahaʼ) and His blessing (barakah), His righteousness (birr) and His insight (basirah); the sin (s) is His loftiness (sana'), His exaltedness (sumuw), and His lordship (siyadah); the mim (m) is His glory (majd), His kingdom (mamlakah), and His favour (manna). This is the view of al-Kalbi.

(p. 50)

The second: the ba' is "free of offspring" (bari' min al-awlad); the sin is "hearer of voices" (sami' al-aswat); the mim is "responder to supplications" (mujib al-da'awat). This is the view of Sulayman ibn Yasar.

The third: the ba' is "Creator of creation" (bari' al-khalq); the sin is "concealer of faults" (satir al-'uyub); the mim is "the Bestower" (al-mannan). This is the view of Abu Rawq.

Were this deduction reported from one who is followed in the science of tafsir, it would be disregarded, because it goes beyond what Allah the Exalted has reserved for His names. But since it was said by one who is followed, I have mentioned it despite its remoteness, as a report and not as a verified position, so that the book includes what has been said.

It is said of one who says "bism Allah" that he has "basmala" (said bismillah), in a later coined usage, and it has come in poetry. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

*Laila said "bismillah" the morning I met her,*
*so how excellent is that beloved who says bismillah!*

As for His saying "Allah" (Allah), it is the most specific of His names to Him, because no one other than Him has been named with the name "Allah."

The second interpretation: its meaning is "Do you know anyone similar to Him?" This is the more general of the two interpretations, because it covers both the name and the act.

It is reported from Abu Hanifah that it is the greatest of Allah's names, because no other shares in it.

They differed regarding this name: is it a proper name (ism 'alam) for the Essence, or a derived name from an attribute? There are two views:

The first: it is a proper name for His Essence, not derived from His attributes, because the names of attributes follow the names of the Essence. Therefore there had to be a name specific to the Essence, to be a proper noun, so that the names of attributes and descriptions would be subordinate.

The second view: it is derived from ʼlh (ilah), and by its derivation, its hamza was dropped and its pronunciation was made heavy (tafkhim), becoming Allah.

They differed regarding what ilah is derived from, in two views: The first: it is derived from al-walah (bewilderment or longing), because servants turn to Him (ya'lahuna ilayhi), that is, they seek refuge in Him in their affairs (p. 51)

affairs, so the one to whom they turn is called ilah, just as the one who is followed is called imam.

The second view: it is derived from al-uluhiyyah, which is worship, from their saying: "So-and-so yatallah," meaning he worships. Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

*By Allah, the excellence of the flirtatious women who wear jewellery*
*when they saw the adorned one's (mu'ammah) ...*

*They glorified and sought forgiveness from their worship (ta'alluh).*

That is, from their worship. It has been reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: ﴿and your gods (wa-alihatak)﴾, meaning "and your worship."

Then they differed as to whether the name ilah is derived from the act of worship or from the entitlement to it, in two views: The first: it is derived from the act of worship. On this view, that would not be an inherent eternal attribute of His Essence, since His worship began after the creation of creatures. Whoever held this view denied that Allah the Exalted has always been God, because before creating, He was not worshipped.

The second view: it is derived from the entitlement to worship. On this view, it is an inherent attribute of His Essence, because He has always been entitled to worship, and so He has always been God. This is the more correct of the two views, because if it were derived from the act of worship and not from the entitlement to it, then 'Isa (peace be upon him) would have to be called ilah because the Christians worship him, and idols would have to be called alihah because their adherents worship them. The invalidity of this is evidence that it is derived from the entitlement to worship, not from the act. So our saying "ilah" on this view is an attribute of the Essence, and on the first view it is an attribute of the act.

As for "al-Rahman al-Rahim," they are two names of Allah the Exalted, and al-Rahim in them is a name derived from His attribute.

As for al-Rahman, there are two views: The first: it is a Hebrew name that has been Arabized, and it is not Arabic, just as al-fustat is a Roman word Arabized, and al-istabraq is a Persian word Arabized. This is because the Quraysh, who were the most astute and eloquent of the Arabs, did not know it until it was mentioned to them, and they said what Allah the Exalted related of them: ﴿And what is the Most Gracious? Shall we prostrate to what you command us? And it increased them in aversion﴾ [al-Furqan 25:60]. This is the view of Tha'lab, who cited the verse of Jarir:

*Will you abandon your migration to the two Qassin (the two mountains)*
*and your wiping over their backs (of the dead) "Rahman" of offerings?*

He said: For this reason He combined al-Rahman with al-Rahim, so that confusion would be removed. According to this view, the original arrangement would be to put al-Rahim before al-Rahman for its Arabic character, but He put al-Rahman first for its emphasis (mubalaghah).

The second view: al-Rahman is an Arabic name like al-Rahim, because their letters are intermixed, and this appears in the speech of the Arabs, and their poetry includes it. al-Shanfara said:

*Did that girl not strike her young camel?*
*Did not my Lord, the Most Gracious, strike her right hand?*

If the two are Arabic names, then they are both derived from mercy (rahmah), and mercy is a favour upon the one in need. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:107], meaning a favour upon them. A favour is called mercy because it comes from mercy.

Al-Rahman is more emphatic than al-Rahim, because al-Rahman's wording and meaning both extend (its effect), whereas al-Rahim's wording does not extend, only its meaning does. For this reason a people were named al-Rahim, but no one was named al-Rahman. The Jahiliyyah used to call Allah the Exalted by it, and the verse of al-Shanfara is upon this. Then Musaylimah the Liar named himself al-Rahman, and he took it from the names of Allah the Exalted. 'Ata' said: For this reason Allah the Exalted paired it with al-Rahim, because no one had named himself "al-Rahman al-Rahim," so that His name would be distinguished from the name of another; the difference then lies in emphasis. Abu 'Ubaydah distinguished between them, saying: al-Rahman is the one possessing mercy, and al-Rahim is the one who shows mercy.

They differed regarding the derivation of al-Rahman and al-Rahim, in two views: The first: both are derived from one mercy, and the wording al-Rahman was made more emphatic than al-Rahim.

The second view: they are derived from two mercies, and the mercy from which al-Rahman is derived is other than the mercy from which al-Rahim is derived, so that the two names are distinct and the two attributes differ. Those who held this view differed regarding the two mercies in three views: The first: al-Rahman is derived from Allah's mercy toward all His creation, and al-Rahim is derived from Allah's mercy toward the people of His obedience.

The second view: al-Rahman is derived from Allah the Exalted's mercy toward the people of this world and the Hereafter, and al-Rahim is derived from His mercy toward the people of this world only, not the Hereafter.

The third view: al-Rahman is derived from the mercy that Allah the Exalted alone possesses, to the exclusion of His servants, and al-Rahim is derived from the mercy that is found in servants in a similar form.

**The Word of the Exalted, the Majestic: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.** As for ﴿All praise is due to Allah﴾, *al-hamd* (praise) is commendation of the one praised for his beautiful attributes and actions. *Al-shukr* (gratitude) is commendation of Him for His bounties. Every gratitude is praise, but not every praise is gratitude. This is the difference between *al-hamd* and *al-shukr*. For this reason, it is permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to praise Himself, but it is not permissible for Him to thank Himself.

As for the difference between *al-hamd* and *al-madh* (eulogy), praise is only deserved for a good act (p-٥٤), whereas eulogy may be for an act or for something other than an act. So every praise is eulogy, but not every eulogy is praise. For this reason, it is permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to be eulogized for His attribute, that He is Knowing and Able, but it is not permissible for Him to be praised for it, because knowledge and power are among the attributes of His essence, not among the attributes of His acts. It is permissible for Him to be eulogized and praised for His attribute that He is the Creator and the Provider, because creation and provision are among the attributes of His acts, not among the attributes of His essence.

As for His words ﴿Lord (*Rabb*)﴾, its derivation has been disputed, with four opinions:

The first: it is derived from *al-malik* (owner), as one says *rabb al-dar*, meaning its owner.

The second: it is derived from *al-sayyid* (master), since the master is called *rabb*. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿As for one of you, he will give his master (*rabbahu*) wine to drink﴾ [Yusuf: 41], meaning his master.

The third opinion: *al-Rabb* is the one who manages (*al-mudabbir*). From this is the saying of Allah, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿and the rabbis (*al-rabbaniyyun*) and the rabbis of the scholars﴾, who are the scholars. They were called *rabbaniyyun* because they manage people through their knowledge. It was also said: *rabbat al-bayt* (the mistress of the house), because she manages it.

The fourth opinion: *al-Rabb* is derived from *al-tarbiyah* (upbringing). From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], so He called the wife's child *rabiba* (stepdaughter), because the husband raises her.

Based on this, the attribute of Allah, exalted is He, as *Rabb*, because He is Owner or Master, is an attribute of His essence. If it is said that it is because He manages His creation and raises them, then it is an attribute of His acts. And when you attach the *alif* and *lam* to it (i.e., *al-Rabb*), it is restricted to Allah, exalted is He, to the exclusion of His servants. If they are removed from it (i.e., *rabb*), it becomes shared between Allah and His servants.

As for His words ﴿the worlds (*al-'alamin*)﴾, it is the plural of *'alam*, which has no singular from its own form, like *rahṭ* and *qawm* (both collective nouns). The people of every age are an *'alam*. Al-'Ajjaj said:

*... ... ... ∗∗∗ Khindif is the chief of this world*

Scholars differ regarding *al-'alam* (the world), with three opinions:

The first: it is everything that has intellect, from angels, humans and jinn. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: the world is this lower world and what is in it.

The third: the world is everything that Allah, exalted is He, created in this world and the Hereafter. This is the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj.

They differed regarding its derivation in two ways. One: it is derived from *al-'ilm* (knowledge). This is the interpretation of those who made *al-'alam* a name for what has intellect.

The second: it is derived from *al-'alamah* (sign), because it is a proof of its Creator. This is the interpretation of those who made *al-'alam* a name for every created thing.

The second: the world is this lower world and what is in it.

The third: the world is everything that Allah, exalted is He, created in this world and the Hereafter. This is the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj.

The second: it is derived from *al-'alamah* (sign), because it is a proof of its Creator. This is the interpretation of those who made *al-'alam* a name for every created thing.

The Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read (مالِكِ, *māliki*), and the rest read (مَلِكِ, *maliki*). Both readings are derived from a common root, and there are two views on that derivation.

The first is that both derive from hardness (al-shiddah), from the saying "malaktu al-'ajina" (مَلَكْتُ العَجِينَ), meaning "I kneaded the dough vigorously."

The second is that both derive from power (al-qudrah). The poet said:

*Malaktu bihā kaffī fa-anharttu fatqahā*
*Yarā qā'imun min dūnihā mā warā'ahā*

I held it in my hand and tore open its opening,
so that one standing outside could see what lay behind it.

The difference between *al-mālik* and *al-malik* is in two respects. The first: *al-mālik* is one who has particular ownership, while *al-malik* is one who has general ownership (sovereignty). The second: *al-mālik* is one specially connected to the sovereignty of the kings (malik al-mulūk), while *al-malik* is one connected to the executive authority of command.

Scholars differ on which of the two is more eloquent in praise, in three views.

The first: *al-malik* is more eloquent in praise than *al-mālik*, because every king is an owner, but not every owner is a king, and because the command of the king takes effect over the owner.

The second: *māliki* is more eloquent in praise than *maliki*, because one may be a king over those he does not own, as one says "malik al-'Arab" (king of the Arabs) and "malik al-Rum" (king of the Romans), even though he does not own them. One is not an owner except over those he owns. Also, a king may be over people and others.

The third, which is the view of Abu Hatim, is that *māliki* is more eloquent in praising the Creator than *maliki*, while *maliki* is more eloquent in praising the created than *māliki*. The difference between them is that a created owner may not be a king, whereas if Allah the Exalted is an owner, He is a king. If Allah the Exalted is described as *malik*, that is one of the attributes of His essence. If He is described as *mālik*, that is one of the attributes of His actions.

As for the Word of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿the Day of Judgment﴾, there are two interpretations of it. The first is that it refers to recompense (al-jazā'). The second is that it refers to reckoning (al-ḥisāb).

As for the linguistic origin of *al-dīn* (الدِّين), there are two views.

The first is custom (al-'ādah). From this is the saying of al-Mutaqqib al-'Abdi:

*Taqūlu wa-qad dara'tu lahā wiḍīnī*
*Ahādhā dīnuhu abadan wa-dīnī*

She says, when I have pushed back her saddle girth:
"Is this his custom forever, and is it mine?"

That is, "his custom and my custom."

The second is that the origin of *al-dīn* is obedience (al-ṭā'ah). From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma:

*La-in ḥalalta bijaww fī Banī Asadin*
*Fī dīni 'Amrin wa-mālat baynanā Fadak*

Even if you alight in the open land among Banu Asad,
under the authority of 'Amr, and Fadak inclines between us.

That is, "in the obedience of 'Amr."

Regarding this Day, there are two views. The first is that it is a day that begins at the rising of dawn and ends at the setting of the sun.

The second is that it is a time of light that continues until Allah the Exalted has reckoned all His creation, after which the people of Paradise settle in Paradise and the people of the Fire settle in the Fire.

Regarding the specification of His ownership of the Day of Judgment, there are two interpretations. The first is that it is a day in which there is no sovereignty other than His. Thus it is greater than the sovereignty of this world, which kings possess. This is the view of al-Asamm.

The second is that when He said ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, He meant by it the sovereignty of this world. Then He said after it ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾, meaning by it the sovereignty of the Hereafter, so that He would combine the sovereignty of this world and the Hereafter.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿You alone do we worship, and You alone do we ask for help﴾. His words, ﴿You alone﴾, are a kināyah (allusive reference) to the name of Allah the Exalted. On this there are two opinions. The first is that the name of Allah the Exalted is in the genitive, governed by the kāf, and this is the view of al-Khalīl (al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad al-Farāhīdī). The second is that it is a single word used as a pronoun referring to the name of Allah the Exalted, with no genitive construction, because a pronoun is not put in the genitive. This is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsaṭ).

As for His words, ﴿we worship﴾, there are three interpretations. The first is that ʿibādah (worship) is submission, which none deserves except Allah the Exalted, because it is the highest degree of submission, and so none deserves it except the One who bestows the greatest favours, such as life, reason, hearing and sight. The second is that ʿibādah is obedience. The third is that it is seeking nearness through obedience.

The first is the most apparent of these, because the Christians worshipped ʿIsā (peace be upon him), yet they did not obey him in worship, whereas the Prophet (ﷺ) is obeyed, and he is not worshipped through obedience.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 1, verses 6–7:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ to the end of it.

As for His saying, ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾, there are two interpretations of it. The first: its meaning is "direct us and show us the way" (irshad wa dalala).

The second: its meaning is "grant us success" (tawfiq), and this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

As for al-Sirat (the path), there are two interpretations. The first: it is the straight way (al-sabil al-mustaqim), and from this is the verse of Jarir:

؎ The Commander of the Believers is upon a path that, when the watering places are crooked, is straight.

The second: it is the clear road. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not sit on every path, threatening﴾ [al-A'raf: 86]. And the poet said:

؎ ... ... ... ∗∗∗ ∗∗∗ so he turned away from the approach of the direct path

It is derived from mustarat al-ta'am (the passage of food), which is its passage in the throat.

Regarding the supplication for this guidance, there are three interpretations. The first: they asked for the continuation of guidance, even though they had already been guided.

The second: its meaning is "increase us in guidance." (p-59)

The third: they asked for it out of sincerity in their desire and hope for the reward of supplication.

They differed over the intended meaning of the straight path, in four sayings. The first: it is the Book of Allah, exalted is He; this is the view of Ali and Abdullah, and something similar is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: it is Islam; this is the view of Jabir ibn Abdullah and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya.

The third: it is the guiding path to the religion of Allah, exalted is He, which has no crookedness in it; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: it is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the best of his household and companions; this is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri and Abu al-Aliyah al-Riyahi.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾, there are five sayings. The first: they are the angels.

The second: they are the prophets. (p-60)

The third: they are the believers in the earlier scriptures.

The fourth: they are the Muslims; this is the view of Waki'.

The fifth: they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him among his companions; this is the view of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

Umar ibn al-Khattab and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr read: (ṣirāṭa man an'amta 'alayhim).

As for His saying, ﴿not of those who have incurred anger, nor of those who are astray﴾, it is narrated from Adi ibn Hatim, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about those who have incurred anger, and he said: 'They are the Jews,' and about those who are astray, and he said: 'They are the Christians.'" (p-61)

This is the view of all the exegetes.

Regarding the anger of Allah upon them, there are four sayings. The first: it is the anger known among servants.

The second: it is the intention of retribution, because the original meaning of anger in the language is harshness, and this attribute is not permissible for Allah, exalted is He.

The third: His anger upon them is His blaming of them.

The fourth: it is a kind of punishment called anger, just as His blessings are called mercy.

Misguidance is the opposite of guidance. Allah, exalted is He, singled out the Jews for anger because they are more intense in enmity.

Umar ibn al-Khattab read: (ghayri al-maghdubi 'alayhim wa ghayri al-ḍāllīn).

The second: its meaning is "grant us success" (tawfiq), and this is the view of Ibn Abbas.
